name: Theodore Roosevelt Island
author: author-C-2026-10-18
summary:
Theodore Roosevelt Island is a wooded island in the Potomac River that serves as the nation’s memorial to its 26th president; the Park Service’s 2015 foundation document calls its Memorial Plaza the only monument to Roosevelt in Washington, D.C. Trails cross upland forest, swamp and tidal marsh, and the same document says the island holds the largest naturally occurring tidal wetland in the District and plants and animals that are rare in the region. It measures 70 acres by the foundation document’s count; the 2004 park brochure gives 88.5 acres for the island together with adjacent Little Island. [1] [2]

The Roosevelt Memorial Association bought the island in October 1931, according to the 2016 Cultural Landscapes Inventory (the brochure dates the purchase to 1932), and gave it to the federal government; Congress established the memorial on May 21, 1932. Landscape architects Frederick Law Olmsted, Jr., and Henry Vincent Hubbard designed it as a living memorial, a native woodland meant to mature over decades and centuries into a “climax” forest that would honor Roosevelt’s conservation record. Architect Eric Gugler designed the plaza and sculptor Paul Manship its bronze statue of Roosevelt, set among four granite tablets carrying Roosevelt’s words on citizenship; it was dedicated in October 1967. [3] [1] [2]

The forest covers an older history. The island has been called My Lord’s Island, Barbadoes, Analostan and Mason’s Island; it was a Native American fishing place, a plantation, a Union Army camp and a camp for people freed from slavery before it was a memorial. The foundation document lists the remnants of American Indian habitation, farmsteads and Civil War encampments as part of its archeological record. [3] [1]

indigenous.html: People were on the island long before any European claim. The National Register nomination quoted in the 2016 landscape inventory says pottery sherds, fire-cracked rock, projectile points and stone flakes found there suggest intensive, long-term prehistoric use, and that through the 18th century the Potomac valley was a meeting place where members of the Five Nation Iroquois traded with Algonquian-speaking peoples whose fishing and farming villages lined the river. The English captain Henry Fleet described Necostin Indians in the area in the 1620s and 1630s, and the nomination adds that the name Analostan likely derives from the Necostin (Anacostian). The park brochure says the island served as a seasonal fishing village. The record is thin: the nomination calls the past survey work small and substandard, and judges the published account of a 1967 excavation inadequate. [3] [2]

slavery.html: From about 1792 until a bank foreclosed on him in 1833, John Mason, son of George Mason of Gunston Hall, ran the island as a small plantation estate, with a neoclassical mansion, fields, livestock and terraced gardens. The National Register nomination says Mason probably relied on slave labor to build, farm and maintain the estate; its statement of significance says the estate was almost certainly run by slave labor. Slave quarters and workshops stood south of the house, some along the walled eastern shore, and cotton and maize were planted to the north. Newspapers in 1902 and 1907 described the overgrown ruins, among them buildings identified as slave quarters. The nomination counts slave sites from the Mason era among the island’s likely archeological resources. [3]

black.html:
Early in the Civil War an employment depot for people who had escaped slavery — “contraband,” in the term of the time — was set up on the island. In the summer of 1863 it quartered and trained the 1st United States Colored Troops, an infantry regiment of free Black men and men who had escaped slavery, the District of Columbia’s Black regular Army regiment, which went on to fight mainly in Virginia and the Carolinas. [3] [1]

From May 1864 the island became a refugee camp for recently freed people and other Black people arriving in the area. They were housed in the empty barracks and told to make do with limited supplies; the inventory records that many died there from lack of basic supplies, disease and overcrowding. An 1864 inspection counted seven barracks and noted plans for a schoolroom and meeting house. The camp was disbanded in June 1865. [3]

labor_ccc.html: The park brochure credits Olmsted and the Civilian Conservation Corps with creating the island’s mature woodland. [2] From 1934 to 1937, Frederick Law Olmsted, Jr., directed young CCC men in clearing most of the non-native vegetation, including most of what remained of John Mason’s plantings, and in planting about 20,000 native hardwood trees and shrubs. In 1936 a Historic American Buildings Survey team recorded the remains of Mason’s mansion before they were removed; CCC crews did the digging. The National Register nomination, quoted in the inventory, notes that the exploration was assigned to a Park Service architect with no archeological training, who was given 12 weeks. The Olmsted firm’s general plan for the island was completed in 1945. [3]
